I’m 55 this year, and my back isn’t what it used to be. With only my wife and me in the household, I have to be practical about labor and input costs. Our 40 mu farm in Quzhou has good loamy soil, and the well gives us reliable water, though I don’t waste electricity on unnecessary irrigation.

This year I’ll keep 30 mu in the wheat-maize double-cropping system that’s been the backbone of our farm. The winter wheat is already in the ground from last October. I’ll use an improved certified seed—the kind the county supply shop recommends, like the Jimai varieties—and manage it with three irrigations: green-up, jointing, and grain filling. Two pesticide applications are enough: a spring herbicide and a fungicide spray at heading if the humidity rises. After harvest in early June, I’ll quickly rotary-till and plant summer hybrid maize. Maize is less fussy; I’ll irrigate it twice, at the big trumpet stage and grain filling, and spray herbicide plus one insecticide if worms show up.

I’ll dedicate the remaining 10 mu to cotton because Quzhou soil grows good cotton, but at my age I can’t handle much more than that—picking still falls heavily on us. I’ll deep-plough that plot in April and plant a hybrid Bt variety to cut down on bollworm damage. Cotton needs more potassium for the bolls, so I’ll push potash there. I’ll irrigate three times and spray four times for aphids, mites, and the occasional pest that Bt doesn’t catch.

For fertilizer, I know our land’s fertility after 30 years. I don’t chase record yields with excessive inputs—stable margins matter more. I expect around 520 kg/mu for wheat, 600 kg/mu for maize, and 260 kg/mu of seed cotton. Those are honest targets for a normal weather year.
